## The Premise

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5;"}
* A coding agent is a **collaborator with no memory**
* The way I use it: Not to write the code, but to help me find it. It is **what work can I delegate, and how do I check it?**
* Three things make delegation safe: a **repository** (so every change is visible and reversible), an **instruction file** (so the agent knows the project), and a **habit of verification** (so you catch what it got wrong).
* Today is a **walkthrough** on one public repo and one real research question — follow along if you like, or just watch and take the repo home.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.68em; margin-top: 1.1em; border-left: 3px solid #2a78d6; padding-left: 0.9em; color: #3d3d3d; line-height: 1.55;"}
**Three goals**

1. See the whole loop once — **clone, branch, diff, undo** — on a real project.
2. See how an agent comes to **know a project** through an instructions file.
3. Watch one substantive question get answered, and watch us **check the machine's work**.
:::

## The Day

::: {.item-list}
- [Framing]{.tag} What agents do, and where they fail silently
- [Setup]{.tag} GitHub, Copilot, Claude Code, Codespaces

# Framing {.divider}

## What a Language Model Is

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5;"}
Start with a model you already estimate. The outcome is the **next token**; the
categories are a fixed vocabulary of perhaps 100,000 of them. That is a
**multinomial logit**:

$$\Pr(w_t = k \mid \text{context}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}_t'\boldsymbol{\beta}_k)}{\sum_j \exp(\mathbf{x}_t'\boldsymbol{\beta}_j)}$$

Everything else is a solution to one problem: **what is $\mathbf{x}_t$?** The context is a
sequence of arbitrary length, not a fixed design matrix.
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[The neural network is learned measurement]{.exp-head}

A layer is a set of **latent variables** — linear combinations passed through a
nonlinearity — and the next layer takes those as its indicators. Stack ~100 of them and
you have learned a representation instead of specifying one. **Attention** makes the
coefficients context-dependent: each token's features are a weighted average of the
other tokens', with weights estimated from the sequence itself. A varying-coefficient
model, fit rather than imposed. "Bank" near *river* is not "bank" near *loan*.
:::

## Two Estimation Stages

::: {.item-list}
- [Pretraining]{.tag} MLE by stochastic gradient descent on trillions of tokens. Billions of parameters, no closed form, no standard errors, no identification claim — the parameters are not interpretable and were never meant to be
- [Alignment]{.tag} A reward model is fit to human pairwise comparisons — a **Bradley–Terry** model of "which answer is better" — then the policy is shifted toward preferred completions
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[Why this matters for how you use it]{.exp-head}

Fluency and instruction-following come from the *second* stage. Factual accuracy is in
neither loss function. The object is a **conditional distribution over text, sampled at
temperature** — so it is a predictive model, run far out of sample, with no uncertainty
estimate attached. It will produce a plausible variable name, a plausible citation, and
a plausible coefficient with equal confidence. That is the whole case for verification.
:::

# Setup {.divider}

## Why a Repository at All

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5;"}
GitHub hosts code, data, and documents on the web. Four reasons it matters for research:

* **Transparency** — the work is open to inspection.
* **Reproducibility** — others can recreate and extend your analysis.
* **Collaboration** — several people contribute to one project without emailing files.
* **Version control** — every change is tracked, and reverting is trivial.
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[And for working with agents]{.exp-head}

An agent edits files in place. The repository is what makes that safe: you can see
exactly what it changed (`git diff`), and undo it (`git restore`). Without version
control, you are letting a confident stranger type into your dissertation.
:::

## The Repository

::: {.tight-code}
```
UNM_Workshop/
├── AGENTS.md              the brief every AI agent reads
├── CLAUDE.md              one line: @AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only)
│   └── wss_clean.rds      built by R/01_recode.R
├── codebooks/             2020 & 2024 survey codebooks (PDF)
├── R/
│   ├── functions.R        pure helpers, shared and unit-tested
│   ├── 00_build_data.R    raw Stata → csv (instructor only)
│   ├── 01_recode.R        all recoding lives here
│   └── 02_analysis.R      models and figures → output/
├── app/app.R              Shiny explorer
├── tests/testthat/        test-unit-* and test-integration-*
├── slides/                these slides
└── .devcontainer/         one-click Codespace
```
:::

::: {.slide-note}
Numbered scripts, one job each, strict order. **Recodes never live in analysis scripts** —
that single rule is what keeps four people and an agent from quietly disagreeing about
what `latino` means.
:::

## Accounts and Tools

::: {.item-list}
- [GitHub]{.tag} Account at [github.com](https://github.com). Students and faculty: [education.github.com](https://education.github.com) for free Copilot Pro
- [Git]{.tag} macOS `xcode-select --install` · Windows [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com)
- [Identity]{.tag} `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`, once
- [Auth]{.tag} [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), then `gh auth login`
- [Copilot]{.tag} VS Code extensions, or RStudio → Tools → Global Options → Copilot
- [Claude]{.tag} `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then `claude` in the repo
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Copilot reads `.github/copilot-instructions.md`; Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`. In this repo both point at `AGENTS.md`, so every tool gets the same brief.
:::

## No Local Install? Use a Codespace

::: {style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.55;"}
On the repository page: **Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main**.

The container in `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` gives you R and tidyverse, RStudio
Server on port 8787, Quarto, Copilot, and Claude Code — in a browser tab, identical for
everyone in the room.
:::

::: {.limits}
[Housekeeping]{.limits-head}
The free tier is 60 core-hours a month. **Stop your codespace when you are done** —
it bills while it idles.
:::

::: {.turn}
[Follow along, if you like]{.turn-head}
1. Open the repository and start a codespace (or clone locally).
2. In the terminal: `gh auth status` — are you signed in?
3. Start `claude`, then type `/init` and read what it writes about this project.
:::

# Git {.divider}

## The Model

::: {.pipeline}
::: {.stage}
[Working directory]{.name}

[edit]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[Staging area]{.name}

[git add]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[Local repository]{.name}

[git commit]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[GitHub]{.name}

[git push]{.sub}
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5;"}
Changes move left to right, one deliberate step at a time, and come back with
`git pull`. The staging area exists so that you commit *some* of your changes — the
finished recode, not the half-written one beside it.
:::

## Clone, and Fork for Later

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-trad}
[CLONE — today]{.card-label}

A copy of a repository **on your computer**, made with `git clone <url>`.

- Needs only read access; this repo is public
- Commit, branch, break things — it stays local
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-subv}
[FORK — for later]{.card-label}

A copy **under your account**, made on the GitHub website.

- For contributing where you lack write access
- Fork + clone + pull request = open-source collaboration
:::
:::

::::

::: {.slide-note}
Today: **clone**. The repository is public, so you only need read access — nobody has to
be added to anything, and nothing you do locally can affect the original. Forking is for
the day you want to send work back somewhere.
:::

## Get the Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git
cd UNM_Workshop
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5; margin-top: 0.6em;"}
From RStudio you can do all of this in **Tools → Terminal → New Terminal**, or
point-and-click in the **Git** tab. The commands are the same underneath, and the
terminal is what you will be able to explain to a collaborator — or to an agent.
:::

## The Everyday Loop

```bash
git pull                        # pick up changes to the original
git status                      # what did I change?
git add R/01_recode.R           # stage specific files, not `git add .` blindly
git commit -m "Add generation recode"
git diff HEAD~1                 # read what you just committed
```

::: {.exp-block}
[What a commit is]{.exp-head}

A snapshot of your changes with a unique ID and a message. The message is for the
version of you who, in four months, needs to know why `age_group` has four categories.
Write it for that person.
:::

::: {.slide-source}
`pull`, `add`, `commit` and `diff` all work in your own clone, with no write access to anything. `push` is the only one that needs somewhere you can write.
:::

## Branching in Your Own Clone

```bash
git switch -c trying-something     # a branch costs nothing
# ...edit, add, commit...
git switch main                    # back to where you started
git branch -D trying-something     # throw the experiment away
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
This is the whole safety net, and it is entirely local — no account, no permissions, no
collaborators. Let the agent loose on a branch; if the result is wrong, delete the
branch.
:::

::: {.limits}
[Rules of the road]{.limits-head}
Branch per task, never commit on `main` · small commits with clear messages · never
commit data you were not given, passwords, or `.Renviron`.
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Pushing, forks and pull requests matter when you share a repo with someone. Not needed today — you only need to read this one.
:::

## When to Use What

::: {.cmd-table}
| Action | When | Command | Needs access? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Clone** | Reading and running someone's code | `git clone <url>` | no |
| **Pull** | Picking up later changes | `git pull` | no |
| **Branch** | Any change you are not sure of | `git switch -c name-topic` | no |
| **Add** | Choosing what goes in the commit | `git add R/01_recode.R` | no |
| **Commit** | Saving a coherent step locally | `git commit -m "message"` | no |
| **Diff** | Checking what the agent did | `git diff` | no |
| **Fork** | You want to send work back | `gh repo fork <repo> --clone` | your account |
| **Push** | Publishing a branch | `git push -u origin name-topic` | write |
| **Pull request** | Asking for review and a merge | `gh pr create --fill` | write on a fork |
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Everything above the line is all you need today — and all you need to use an agent safely on any repository, including your own.
:::

## Conflicts and Undo

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
**A conflict looks like this**

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> main
```

Keep what is right, delete the markers, then `git add` and `git commit`. You may ask the
agent — *"resolve the conflict in `R/01_recode.R`, keeping both recodes"* — and then
**read the diff**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.cmd-table}
| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard edits to a file | `git restore file.R` |
| Unstage | `git restore --staged file.R` |
| Fix the last message | `git commit --amend` |
| Undo a pushed commit | `git revert <hash>` |
| See what changed | `git diff` |
:::
:::

::::

# Agents {.divider}

## How an Agent Sees This Repository

::: {style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.5;"}
1. **On start it loads instruction files**: `CLAUDE.md` (Claude Code), `AGENTS.md`
   (Copilot, Codex, Cursor, and others), `.github/copilot-instructions.md` (Copilot).
2. **It reads what you point at** — `@R/01_recode.R` — or what it finds by searching.
3. **It runs commands** — R, git, shell — with your permission.
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[So the instruction file is the project brief]{.exp-head}

Layout, variable meanings, conventions, guardrails. Here `CLAUDE.md` contains one line,
`@AGENTS.md`, so every tool in the room shares a single source of truth. Change the
brief once and all of them follow it.
:::

## Anatomy of a Good `AGENTS.md`

::: {.tight-code}
```markdown
## Project
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump from 2020
to 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?

## Layout
- data/wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only; never edit by hand)
- R/01_recode.R           all recoding lives here
- codebooks/              cite these when describing a variable

## Rules
- R + tidyverse, native pipe |>. Minimal comments.
- New recodes go in R/01_recode.R, not in analysis scripts.
- Always report n_obs and n_miss with any model.
- Use survey weights for population estimates; say when you don't.
- Don't push to main without the user's say-so; prefer a branch + PR.
```
:::

::: {.slide-note}
What the project is · where things live · which files are read-only · variable
definitions and where to **cite** them · conventions · guardrails. Keep it short:
agents follow concise rules far better than essays.
:::

## Claude Code: What You Actually Type

::: {.cmd-table}
| Command | Does | Command | Does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/init` | Draft a `CLAUDE.md` | `/review` | Review a pull request |
| `/memory` | Edit instruction files | `/permissions` | What it may run unasked |
| `/agents` | Build subagents | `/resume` | Return to a session |
| `/clear` | Fresh context (cheap) | `/mcp` | Connect external tools |
| `/compact` | Summarize a long session | `@file` | Put a file in context |
| `/model` | Switch model | `!cmd` | Run a shell command |
| `/cost` `/usage` | Track spending | <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> | Cycle plan / auto-accept |
:::

::: {.slide-source}
<kbd>Esc</kbd> interrupts; <kbd>Esc</kbd> <kbd>Esc</kbd> rewinds the conversation. A subagent worth building today: a *codebook checker* that reads a recode and the PDF and reports disagreements.
:::

## Copilot: What You Actually Type

::: {.cmd-table}
| Key / command | Does |
|---|---|
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> / <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Accept / dismiss an inline suggestion |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> | Inline chat on the selection |
| `/explain` `/fix` `/tests` `/doc` | Chat commands on what you have open |
| `@workspace` `#file` | Add the repo, or one file, to context |
| Agent mode | Multi-file edits that run commands |
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[Division of labor]{.exp-head}

Copilot is strongest at the **next line** — completions while you type. Claude Code is
strongest at the **next task** — "add income terciles to the recode, rerun it, and show
me what changed." Use both.
:::

## Spending Less

::: {.item-list}
- [Clear]{.tag} `/clear` between unrelated tasks — long context is re-billed every turn
- [Point]{.tag} Name files (`@R/02_analysis.R`) instead of asking it to look around
- [Plan]{.tag} Plan mode for anything large: approve the plan, then let it execute
- [Downshift]{.tag} A smaller model for routine edits and renames
- [Batch]{.tag} One well-specified request beats six vague corrections
:::

## Verify, Always

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-do}
[DELEGATE]{.card-label}

- Scaffolding and boilerplate
- Refactoring you can read
- Documentation and tests
- Debugging an error message
- "Explain what this script does"
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-dont}
[NEVER TRUST UNCHECKED]{.card-label}

- Variable coding and reverse-coding
- Which cases got dropped
- Weights and survey design
- Anything citing a number
- Anything citing a source
:::
:::

::::

::: {.slide-note}
The minimum check, every time: **read the diff**, confirm the coding against the
codebook, and look at `n_obs` and `n_miss`. If the N moved and nobody said why,
something was silently dropped.
:::

# The Pipeline {.divider}

## The Question

::: {style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.55;"}
**Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, and
does authoritarianism condition that shift?**

Western States Survey (YouGov), 2020 and 2024: Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico,
Utah. Latino is the YouGov `race` item; authoritarianism is the mean of four
child-rearing pairs, scored 0–1 with 1 the authoritarian response.
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Variable definitions and coding: `codebooks/wss2020_codebook.pdf`, `codebooks/wss2024_codebook.pdf`, and the variable list in `AGENTS.md`. Cite the codebook, not the agent.
:::

## One Stage, One Script

::: {.pipeline}
::: {.stage}
[00 build]{.name}

[raw Stata → csv]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[01 recode]{.name}

[csv → wss_clean.rds]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[02 analysis]{.name}

[models → output/]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[app]{.name}

[Shiny explorer]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[publish]{.name}

[quarto → gh-pages]{.sub}
:::
:::

::: {.cmd-table}
| Stage | File | Owner today | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| Build | `R/00_build_data.R` | instructor | `data/wss_2020_2024.csv` |
| Recode | `R/01_recode.R` | recode team | `data/wss_clean.rds` |
| Analyze | `R/02_analysis.R` | analysis team | `output/*.png`, model summaries |
| Explore | `app/app.R` | Shiny team | interactive app |
| Check | `tests/testthat/` | everyone | pass / fail |
| Publish | `quarto publish gh-pages` | instructor | the website you are reading |
:::

## Run It End to End

```bash
Rscript R/01_recode.R                       # csv  -> data/wss_clean.rds
Rscript R/02_analysis.R                     # models, figures -> output/
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("app")'
```

::: {.exp-block}
[Why this order is enforced]{.exp-head}

Every number in the paper traces back through exactly one path. If the recode changes,
the analysis and the app change with it, because neither one keeps its own private copy
of the recoding logic. Ask the agent to add a recode to `02_analysis.R` and it will
happily do it — this is the rule you are enforcing against your own convenience.
:::

## Where We Start

::: {.cmd-table}
| Weighted two-party Trump share | 2020 | 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-Latino | .503 (n = 1,944) | .511 (n = 2,828) | +.008 |
| Latino | .398 (n = 937) | .419 (n = 786) | +.021 |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.5; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
n_obs = 6,495 two-party voters · n_miss = 1,105 (non-voters, other candidates, ineligible) of 7,600 respondents.
:::

::: {.limits}
[The puzzle]{.limits-head}
A two-point Latino shift, on 786 Latino respondents in 2024, is far from the
double-digit national exit-poll story. Sample? Weights? Mode? Reported versus intended
vote? **That is the interesting part** — not reproducing a headline, but working out what
this sample can and cannot support.
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Produced by `R/02_analysis.R` from `data/wss_clean.rds`; weights are `weight` (2020) and `weight_all` (2024). Confidence intervals in the script use a Kish effective *n*, not a design-based variance.
:::

## Four Things We Can Demonstrate

::: {.item-list}
- [Recode]{.tag} Generations, income terciles, strength of partisanship — each checked against the codebook
- [Analysis]{.tag} `brms` logit; predicted probabilities for authoritarianism × Latino × year. Does `vote_type` (reported vs. intended) matter?
- [Shiny]{.tag} A state-by-year panel and a download button
- [Skeptics]{.tag} Is this sample representative of Latino voters? Weighting, mode, and comparison with external estimates
:::

::: {.slide-note}
We will walk one of these through the whole loop — prompt, diff, `n_obs`, test — and the
rest are here as worked examples you can run later on the repo, or on your own data.
:::

## What `testthat` Is

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.5;"}
R's unit-testing package. A test file is just R code that **asserts** rather than
prints: it says what must be true, and fails loudly when it is not. One file per
concern, in `tests/testthat/`, named `test-*.R`.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.tight-code}
```r
# tests/testthat/test-unit-recode.R
library(testthat)
wss <- readRDS("data/wss_clean.rds")

test_that("auth scale is bounded", {
  expect_true(all(
    wss$authoritarianism >= 0 &
    wss$authoritarianism <= 1,
    na.rm = TRUE))
})
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.5em; color: #6b6b6b; line-height: 1.4;"}
`test_that("what must be true", { expectations })` — the string is the failure message,
so write it as a claim.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cmd-table}
| Expectation | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(x, y)` | equal within tolerance |
| `expect_identical(x, y)` | exactly identical |
| `expect_true(x)` | all of `x` is `TRUE` |
| `expect_setequal(x, y)` | same values, any order |
| `expect_length(x, n)` | length is `n` |
| `expect_error(f())` | it *does* fail |
| `expect_no_warning(f())` | it runs clean |
| `skip("reason")` | not applicable here |
:::
:::

::::

::: {.slide-source}
Run them: `Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'` → `[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 10 ]`. Inside a package it is `devtools::test()`, and `usethis::use_test("recode")` creates the file.
:::

## Unit vs. Integration

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-trad}
[UNIT — `test-unit-*.R`]{.card-label}

One function, **synthetic input written in the test**. Nothing on disk can make it pass or fail.

```r
expect_equal(pid_to_party3(1:7),
  c("Democrat","Democrat","Democrat",
    "Independent","Republican",
    "Republican","Republican"))
```

Milliseconds. Tells you **where** it broke.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-subv}
[INTEGRATION — `test-integration-*.R`]{.card-label}

The pieces together: real CSV, built `.rds`, the live Shiny server.

```r
testServer("app", {
  session$setInputs(by = "latino",
                    wt = TRUE)
  expect_true(all(est()$trump <= 1))
})
```

Seconds. Tells you **that** it broke.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.slide-note}
Unit tests need **units**. A 200-line script has nothing to unit-test — which is why
the pure helpers live in `R/functions.R`. Extracting the function comes first; the
test comes second.
:::

## Make the Agent Prove It

::: {.tight-code}
```r
test_that("authoritarianism is a 0-1 mean of four items", {
  wss <- readRDS("data/wss_clean.rds")
  expect_true(all(wss$authoritarianism >= 0 & wss$authoritarianism <= 1, na.rm = TRUE))
  expect_equal(nrow(wss), 7600)
})

test_that("trump_vote is coded only for two-party voters", {
  wss <- readRDS("data/wss_clean.rds")
  expect_setequal(unique(na.omit(wss$trump_vote)), c(0, 1))
  expect_equal(sum(!is.na(wss$trump_vote)), 6495)
})
```
:::

::: {.slide-note}
A test is how you make a verification **permanent**. Write one for every recode you
accept from an agent: it costs a minute now and catches the silent change six weeks
from now, when somebody "improves" the recode.
:::

## Anatomy of a Shiny App

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.5;"}
Three objects — `ui` (nested HTML widgets), `server` (a function of `input`, `output`,
`session`), and `shinyApp(ui, server)` — and one idea: **reactivity**. You never write
"when the user clicks, recompute." You declare what each output *is*, and Shiny
re-runs what depends on what changed.
:::

::: {.pipeline}
::: {.stage}
[input$by]{.name}

[the control]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[est()]{.name}

[reactive — caches]{.sub}
:::
::: {.stage}
[output$plot]{.name}

[render]{.sub}
:::
:::

::: {.item-list}
- [input$x]{.tag} Read-only, set by the browser. Reading it creates the dependency
- [reactive()]{.tag} Caches, and re-runs only when something it read changed. `est()` is used by both plot and table — computed once
- [render*()]{.tag} An output; re-runs on change and writes into `output$plot`
:::

::: {.limits}
[The two mistakes agents make]{.limits-head}
Calling a reactive outside a reactive context — *"operation not allowed without an
active reactive context"* — and recomputing the same summary in every `render*` block
instead of sharing one `reactive()`.
:::

## The App Holds No Analysis Logic

::: {.tight-code}
```r
source(here::here("R/functions.R"))          # same helpers as the analysis
wss <- read_rds(here::here("data/wss_clean.rds"))   # loads once, outside server

server <- function(input, output, session) {        # session: needed by testServer()
  est <- reactive({
    wss |> filter(state %in% input$state) |> trump_share(input$by, weighted = input$wt)
  })
  output$plot <- renderPlot(ggplot(est(), aes(year, trump, colour = .data[[input$by]], ...)))
  output$tab  <- renderTable(est())
}
```
:::

::: {.item-list}
- [One source of truth]{.tag} The app calls `trump_share()`, the same function the paper calls — it cannot drift
- [`.data[[input$by]]`]{.tag} Tidy evaluation for a column chosen at runtime, not `get()` and not pasted strings
- [n_obs, n_miss on screen]{.tag} Every point has a sample size behind it, and some are small
- [Testable]{.tag} `server` is an ordinary function: `testServer()` sets inputs and reads reactives, no browser
:::

::: {.slide-source}
Running it: `Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("app")'`. The app reads the recode's **output**, never the raw CSV.
:::

# In the Wild {.divider}

## A Bigger Case: The Arizona Voter Project

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.5;"}
Everything so far has been one CSV and three scripts. The same workflow scales: the
[Arizona Voter Project](https://voterproject.arizona.edu) is a public-facing data
project at the University of Arizona — statewide voter file, geocoded addresses,
harmonized surveys, election returns — built and maintained with agent assistance
throughout.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-trad}
[THE PIECES]{.card-label}

- Voter-file and address tables in a **warehouse** (BigQuery), queried from R
- **Geocoding** addresses to tract and block group
- A **harmonized survey panel** for over-time estimates
- **Aggregation** to county / tract / district, with small-cell suppression
- An **Angular widget bundle** ported into the public site
:::
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.contest-card .card-subv}
[WHAT THE AGENT DOES]{.card-label}

- Writes the **query**, the recode, the aggregation — the boilerplate
- Runs **repeatable procedures** captured as skills: "geocode the backlog," "rebuild the widgets"
- Does **not** decide what a measure means, which weight applies, or whether a number is publishable
:::
:::

::::

::: {.slide-note}
The scale changes; the discipline does not. Same three guardrails — a repository, a
written brief, and verification before anything is published.
:::

## Why It Works at That Scale

::: {.item-list}
- [Procedures, not prompts]{.tag} A recurring task — geocode a new build, refresh the aggregates, ship the site bundle — is written down once as a **skill** the agent loads, rather than re-explained each session
- [Cost guards in code]{.tag} A warehouse query **dry-runs** and refuses to scan past a byte budget. The guardrail is in the function, not in the instructions
- [Suppression as a rule]{.tag} Small cells are suppressed in the aggregation step, so no downstream chart can leak one
- [One brief, many repos]{.tag} Each repository carries its own `AGENTS.md`; the agent reads the project before touching it
:::

::: {.exp-block}
[The transferable lesson]{.exp-head}

Agents are most useful where a task is **specified and repeated** — and most dangerous
where a task is **judgment**. The way to get the first without the second is to make
the specified parts executable: a skill, a test, a cost guard, a suppression threshold.
Anything left to prose will eventually be ignored.
:::

::: {.slide-source}
<https://voterproject.arizona.edu> · Structure described by the instructor; no project data appears in this workshop repository.
:::

## {.conclusion}

::: {.kicker}
Wrap-up
:::

::: {.headline}
What to take home
:::

::: {.takeaways}
1. The repository is the safety net. **Branch, diff, revert** — then an agent editing
   your files is a convenience rather than a risk.
2. The instruction file is the real interface. **One brief, every tool**, short enough
   to be followed.
3. Agents are strong where failure is loud and weak where it is **silent**. Research
   code is mostly the second kind.
4. Verification is not optional and not vague: **read the diff, cite the codebook,
   report n_obs and n_miss, write the test.**
5. One pipeline, one path from raw data to the published number.
:::

::: {.close}
**This was a walkthrough, not an assignment.** Everything shown is in the repository:
clone it, run it, and take the workflow — brief, pipeline, diff, test — to your own
project.
:::
